pillar: Osteoid Osteoma RFA: The Minimally Invasive Cure for a Painful Benign Bone Tumour

items.q: What is radiofrequency ablation for osteoid osteoma?
items.a: Radiofrequency ablation, or RFA, uses a thin needle guided by CT scan to heat and destroy the small tumour core, called the nidus, inside your bone. The needle passes through a tiny skin puncture, so no bone is cut away. Heat of roughly 90 degrees Celsius is applied for about six minutes. Most people go home the same day with a single stitch or a plaster.

items.q: Is osteoid osteoma cancer, and can I just take painkillers instead?
items.a: Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone tumour, not cancer, and it does not spread. Some do settle on their own over several years, and anti-inflammatory tablets such as aspirin or ibuprofen control the pain in many people. Long-term tablet use carries its own stomach and kidney risks, which is why RFA is often preferred in young patients. The choice depends on your symptoms and your doctor's advice.

items.q: Does RFA actually cure osteoid osteoma, or does the pain come back?
items.a: RFA cures most osteoid osteomas in a single session, with published success rates of about 90 to 95 percent. The night pain that defines this tumour often disappears within a day or two of the procedure. Around 5 to 10 percent of people have pain return, usually within the first year, and a second ablation can often be done. Your radiologist will confirm whether repeat treatment suits your case.

You will not feel the ablation itself, because it is done under general anaesthesia or spinal anaesthesia. Afterwards most people describe mild soreness at the puncture site for a few days, controlled with simple painkillers. The deep, boring night pain of the osteoid osteoma usually settles far faster than the puncture soreness. Anaesthesia choice depends on your age, the bone involved, and your anaesthetist's assessment.

items.q: How soon can I walk, work or play sport again?
items.a: Most people walk on the same day and return to desk work within two to three days. Because no bone is removed, the treated bone stays strong and does not need a cast or crutches in most cases. Contact sport and heavy running are usually allowed again at four to six weeks. Recovery timing depends on which bone was treated, so follow your own surgeon's advice.

items.q: Is RFA better than open surgery for osteoid osteoma?
items.a: RFA has replaced open surgery as the first choice for most osteoid osteomas because it matches surgical cure rates while removing almost none of the bone. Open surgery can require a large incision, bone grafting, and weeks on crutches; RFA needs a needle puncture and a day. Surgery may still be preferred when the tumour sits within a few millimetres of the spinal cord, a nerve, or the skin.

items.q: What can go wrong with RFA?
items.a: Serious complications are uncommon, occurring in roughly 2 to 3 percent of procedures. The main risks are skin burn where the needle enters, infection, and nerve or cartilage injury when the tumour lies close to those structures. Protective steps such as injecting sterile fluid or carbon dioxide to push nerves away are routine. Ask your interventional radiologist which specific risks apply to the position of your tumour.

items.q: Can RFA be used if the tumour is in my spine?
items.a: Spinal osteoid osteomas can often be ablated, but they need extra care because the nidus may sit close to nerve roots or the spinal cord. Radiologists use thermal protection, nerve monitoring, and sometimes cooled needles to keep heat away from nerve tissue. Tumours less than about one centimetre from the cord may be treated with cryoablation or surgery instead. Suitability depends on imaging review by an experienced centre.

items.q: How much does osteoid osteoma RFA cost in India?
items.a: RFA for osteoid osteoma in India commonly costs between about 2,500 and 5,000 US dollars, including imaging, anaesthesia, and a day-care hospital stay. The same procedure in Europe or the United States often runs several times higher. Prices vary with the hospital, the bone involved, and whether a second session is needed. CancerFax can help you request written quotes from centres, which your treating oncology team should review.

items.q: Do I need to travel abroad, or is treatment available near me?
items.a: Osteoid osteoma RFA is available in most large teaching hospitals with a CT scanner and an interventional radiology unit, so many patients are treated close to home. Travel usually makes sense only when local waiting times are long, the tumour is in a difficult site, or costs are lower elsewhere. If you are considering a centre in India or China, CancerFax can share your scans with them for an opinion.
